verdicts.reason: Derived before running: COMPOSITION.md 2.2 allows evidence names that differ from request names ('use unique evidence field names'). So a renamed binding legitimately produces request names in observed_request and evidence names in actual_fields. RESERVATION-RECORDS.md lines 31 and 33 ('complete operation-field projection', 'the actual operation fields supplied by the observation') require no name equality, and the reservation contract cannot see completion bindings. TypeScript does the same at reservations.ts:287-291. RESERVATION-GAPS-DECISION-20260913.md records 'an observed request that is not the projection of the actual fields is INPUT_INVALID' as decided by the text, so this is that recorded rule implemented as name equality, which the skeptic rules allow reporting. It is not a duplicate. The CONTRACT-DECISIONS entry on foreign partition projection (line 72) states the projection goes through bindings, which supports the finding. No committed case renames a binding (313 case files with evidence_bindings, 0 renamed). I did not probe the foreign path. That part rests on reading lifecycle.py:2160-2205, where the same embedded record reaches the same reservation check.

Text: LIFE-009 table row NOT_SENT/ACCEPTED gives DISPUTED DISPATCH_EVIDENCE_CONFLICT with 'Permit may support a fresh attempt: no'. The same section says 'REJECTED, SENT, UNKNOWN or disputed evidence consumes the permit' and 'A fresh attempt reported NOT_SENT with no accepted acknowledgement on a consumed permit is PREREQUISITE_MISSING'. No other sentence and no CONTRACT-DECISIONS entry (line 75 covers only possibly-sent fresh attempts) carves out a NOT_SENT row with an ACCEPTED acknowledgement. The rerun of python-verify/probe_dispatch.py reproduces the split. The first step is DISPUTED on both. On the second, Python returns STEP DISPATCH_REFUSED [LATE_OR_PROHIBITED_DISPATCH, NATIVE_NOT_SENT] and appends a dispatch record, while TypeScript returns REFUSED PREREQUISITE_MISSING. Cause confirmed by reading: lifecycle.py:941 `consumed = any(row['attempt']['status'] != 'NOT_SENT' ...)` ignores the acknowledgement, while typescript/lifecycle.ts:1235 also counts an ACCEPTED acknowledgement. I rate it major, not blocker: the text is unambiguous, the error is local to Python, and no committed expectation is wrong. It is still reachable with a single-fault history and changes committed state.

Text: AUTHORITY-CHECKS.md 'Deterministic refusal selection' says 'Accumulate directly checkable failures within the phase and select its first code; do not let loop order choose a different result'. The phase-4 order is ACT_CONFLICT, GATE_REQUIRED, EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE, ACT_NOT_AUTHORIZED, ACT_NOT_ACCEPTED. Missing returns follow gate evidence, which makes them EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE. Return-channel failures are ACT_NOT_AUTHORIZED (line 66), and line 27 plus CONTRACT-DECISIONS line 97 place a channel invalid at evaluation in phase 4. Expected: P1a gives EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE and P1b gives ACT_NOT_AUTHORIZED. The rerun of python-verify/probe_auth.py reproduces both splits. P1a: Python ACT_NOT_AUTHORIZED, TypeScript EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE. P1b: Python ACT_NOT_ACCEPTED, TypeScript ACT_NOT_AUTHORIZED. The single-fault controls P1c and P1d agree. Reading authority_acts.py:124-127 shows ACT_NOT_ACCEPTED returned before any return is examined, and the per-return early returns on lines 131-153 let loop order decide. I rate it major: the text is explicit, the defect is in Python, reach is two-fault inputs, and no committed case is wrong.

Text: LIFE-003 says the policy decision has 'subject digest digest("work-class-definition",definition)', that 'Each of the three records has recorded_at no later than the authorization clock', that the 'four distinct evidence identifiers' apply, and that 'Restart recomputes every digest, time relation and binding'. LIFE-019's last paragraph refuses 'any changed digest, missing record, broken binding, status violation ... as STATE_INVALID'. The 'finite invariant set' paragraph in LIFE-019 does not revoke LIFE-003's explicit restart sentence. The rerun of python-verify/probe_deploy.py, which recomputes the full digest chain including the root activation digest, reproduces the gap. All four tampered revision-0 states (policy subject, source PENDING, correspondence after the clock, duplicate evidence ids) return STEP CLOCK_RECORDED on both consumers. Reading lifecycle.py:257-260 confirms that restart rechecks only the three review digests, while it checks the organizational-authorization status, scope and times. Reach is limited to forged or corrupted checkpoints, and no committed case is affected.

The LIFE-003 text maps statuses to EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE and mismatches to BINDING_MISMATCH. It orders these checks only against the organizational-authorization checks and initial_clocks. The general precedence lists (LIFECYCLE.md line 107, PROTOCOL.md line 75) do not reach inside deployment evidence checks, and the CR-01 entry in CONTRACT-DECISIONS sets no order. Sentence order (source subject before policy status) would suggest BINDING_MISMATCH, but no rule makes sentence order normative. The rerun reproduces p6o: Python REFUSED EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE, TypeScript REFUSED BINDING_MISMATCH. Python's order is visible at lifecycle.py _deployment_review_evidence, where all statuses are checked before subjects. I did not verify the side claim about how Python maps correspondence codes. Severity major: the text does not decide, the consumers diverge on an observable refusal code, and reach is limited to two-fault deployments.

RESERVATION-RECORDS.md line 70 makes UNKNOWN_RESERVATION and LATE_EFFECT_AFTER_RELEASE take precedence only 'over the native record's mismatch reason'. The next rule gives clean records 'the first applicable reason in this order, whatever the prior reservation status', ending in MATCHED_EFFECT. Read literally, a clean exact EFFECT against a RELEASED reservation falls under the ordered list, which contradicts table row line 50 ('RELEASED; later EFFECT') and the LATE-applies-only-to-EFFECT sentence. The LATE-applies-only-to-EFFECT sentence came from gaps decision B1; the 'whatever the prior reservation status' wording is not addressed by any recorded decision. The rerun of python-verify/probe_res.py gives EFFECT_DISPUTED [LATE_EFFECT_AFTER_RELEASE] for p9a and p9b on both consumers, so there is no behavior split. Only the wording is defective.

LIFE-009 names only two classes of fresh attempt on a consumed permit: SENT, UNKNOWN or ACCEPTED is retained as DISPUTED, and NOT_SENT without ACCEPTED is PREREQUISITE_MISSING, justified 'because nothing reached the connector'. A REJECTED attempt did reach the connector, and the section also says 'A changed request with attempt REJECTED and no accepted acknowledgement also records DISPUTED: connector rejection does not prove that the changed operation had no effect'. CONTRACT-DECISIONS line 75's rationale ('not grounds for discarding a fact that may have reached the connector') points the same way. A reader could reasonably reach PREREQUISITE_MISSING, a table-driven DISPATCH_REFUSED, or DISPUTED for a changed request. New probes python-verify/probe_rejected.py and probe_rejected2.py add evidence the finding lacked. After a REJECTED first attempt, both consumers refuse a fresh REJECTED/NONE attempt as PREREQUISITE_MISSING, for both an unchanged request and a validly changed request (beneficiary employee-8). The same changed REJECTED request on an unconsumed permit is retained as DISPUTED [NATIVE_ARGUMENT_MISMATCH, NATIVE_DISPATCH_REJECTED] on both. TypeScript lifecycle.ts:1236 matches Python. So the consumers agree, but they discard a changed-argument attempt that the text's own reasoning says to retain. I raise severity from minor to major because a reader can get a different observable result.

findings.title: roe effect decisions carry a BUDGET detail that LIFE-006 does not list for effect observations
findings.text_citation: LIFECYCLE.md line 50: "Authority, separation and budget withholdings carry their corresponding detail. Dispatch observations carry DISPATCH. Effect observations carry EFFECT and also carry ROUTE, LABEL, or LIMIT when that same transition selects a route or stops on a label or limit." The same paragraph: a consumer rejects a missing, duplicate, out-of-order or incompatible detail as STATE_INVALID.
findings.expected_from_text: Read literally, a budget-backed effect decision has details [EFFECT] (unknown, foreign) or [EFFECT, ROUTE] (matched completion). No sentence requires or permits a BUDGET detail on a non-withholding effect decision.
findings.evidence: All four roe effect results carry a BUDGET detail first, for example effect-engage-a-1: [BUDGET {reasons [], receipt_digest, registry_digest}, EFFECT MATCHED, ROUTE]; effect-engage-a-unknown: [BUDGET, EFFECT UNKNOWN] (extract.out lines 290, 350, 359). DERIVATIONS.md item 7 lists the BUDGET detail without citing a rule. A reader who follows LIFE-006 as written omits it and gets different decision bytes, decision_id and state digests. The gap was already raised in review/records/REVIEW-vectors-renewal-budget-20260912.md item 5 for D2-197, D2-241, D2-242, D2-270 and D2-271, and no decision appears in CONTRACT-DECISIONS.md. The convention is corpus-wide, not specific to this specimen.
findings.proposed_fix: Add one sentence to LIFE-006: an effect observation whose transition applies a registry result also carries one BUDGET detail naming that registry and receipt, with the receipt reasons. Alternatively, remove the detail from every effect expectation. Record the decision in CONTRACT-DECISIONS.md.

findings.title: roe-02 cites RA 2.3.1 (1) for barring fire at PDSS, but the source names PDSS as the people the unit protects
findings.text_citation: RA 2.3.1 (ra.txt lines 391-395): you may open fire against an individual who fires or aims his weapon at, or otherwise demonstrates an intent to imminently attack, you, friendly forces, or Persons with Designated Special Status (PDSS) or property with designated special status under your protection.
findings.expected_from_text: In the RoE, PDSS are protected parties whose endangerment justifies fire. The rule says nothing about a PDSS individual being a barred target. The nearest support for treating protected entities as invalid targets is RA 4.3 (ra.txt lines 728-732: protected entities marked as an invalid target). RA 5.5.5 (line 1194) likewise uses protected entity for the object of aggression.
findings.evidence: MAPPING.md line 42 gives roe-02 "A track whose protected status is other than NONE is never a permitted subject" with basis "RA 2.3.1 (1), persons and property with designated special status". The scenario roe-protected-status proposes a target with protected_status PDSS, which puts the source's protected category on the attacker's side. The SEI sources do not support the obligation as attributed.
findings.proposed_fix: Change the roe-02 basis to RA 4.3 (protected entities marked as invalid targets). State that barring fire at a protected track is the specimen's synthetic extension, not a reading of 2.3.1 (1). Consider a target status value other than PDSS.

findings.title: Sepsis time-zero anchor is the alert delivery event time, not the policy's recognition time, and no residue records the difference
findings.location: conformance/work-class/1.0.0-draft.2/specimens/sepsis-surveillance/correspondence-record.json (residue); README.md line 9; DERIVATIONS.md lines 9, 29, 37; valid-trace/requests.jsonl lines 2-5
findings.text_citation: COMPOSITION 5.1: an ancestor declaration is added to the occurred_at instant of the anchor occurrence. LIFE-010 completed-occurrence table: a timely matching success records the native event_time. LIFE-010: attempted_at <= event_time <= observed_at. LIFE-009: attempted_at is no earlier than the permit issuance clock. source-policy.json hour-one-bundle: "Time zero is the alert's recorded recognition time."
findings.expected_from_text: antibiotic-window is due at the raise-alert delivery event_time plus 3600 seconds. That instant can never be earlier than the alert proposal clock, and in practice it follows recognition. The draft-2 construct therefore measures from delivery, not recognition, and the correspondence should record that as residue.
findings.evidence: In the valid trace, clock revision 1, the alert dispatch attempt, the delivery event_time and observed_at are all 2026-09-12T08:00:00Z (probe output in this session). The anchor equals recognition only because every timestamp falls in the same second. README.md line 9 says no residue row records a time-zero mismatch. The residue list holds only UNSUPPORTED provision rows and the EXCLUDED alert cap. A recognition at 07:58 with delivery at 08:01 would move the deadline to 09:01, outside the policy's hour.
findings.proposed_fix: Add a residue row stating that the deadline runs from the alert's delivery event time, which is no earlier than the proposal clock, rather than from recognition. Or separate recognition from delivery in the valid trace and record the gap. Correct the README sentence.

findings.title: Attending-acknowledgement deadline runs from page activation, not from the page, but maps to the fifteen-minutes-of-the-page obligation with no residue

findings.expected_from_text: The deadline is due at the page occurrence's activation (the alert completion, clock 08:00) plus 15 minutes, whenever the page is actually sent. findings.title: roe variant 9 claims instance A's committed effect stands, but the request cannot show it
findings.text_citation: LIFE-008: a later revocation does not erase a still-valid committed permit, reservation, dispatch record or later effect evidence. LIFE-006 precedence: current authority precedes shared-budget revision and policy, so no registry transition occurs.
findings.expected_from_text: The LIFE-008 property needs the revocation observed against the instance or registry that holds the committed record. A withholding on instance B with budget_results [] never touches A's work state and does not return the registry.
findings.evidence: expectations.json state_and_budget_consequence: "the supplied settled registry ... is unchanged, so instance A's committed effect stands". The result carries instance B's state only and empty budget_results (extract.out lines 400-406). The claim is true for every withheld proposal whether or not a revocation occurred. DERIVATIONS.md line 65 concedes the revocation-after-permit case is not exercised, yet MAPPING.md line 24 cites this scenario for committed permits, reservations and occurrences standing.
findings.proposed_fix: Remove "committed effect standing" from the label and from the MAPPING row's claim, or add a request in which the revocation is observed on the instance holding a committed permit or settled reservation.

verdicts.reason: What the text requires, read first. LIFECYCLE.md:50 lists which details go with which events. Only authority, separation and budget withholdings get their own detail. Effect observations get EFFECT plus ROUTE, LABEL or LIMIT. Restart rejects a missing, duplicate or incompatible detail as STATE_INVALID. I searched every .md file in the library: no sentence puts a BUDGET detail on an effect decision that is not a withholding. The lifecycle schema's decisionDetail is a plain oneOf with no rule tying detail kinds to events. The nearest counter-evidence is LIFECYCLE.md:84 ('details carry the underlying records even when the exact reason set is empty') and the :62 row that adds 'every reservation receipt reason'. A reader could take those to imply a BUDGET detail, but neither names the kind, so the text does not settle it and two conforming readers can produce different decision bytes. Evidence reproduced: both consumers return OUTCOME_RETAINED with [BUDGET reasons [], EFFECT] for effect-engage-a-unknown, and DISPUTED with [BUDGET [UNEXPECTED_EFFECT], EFFECT] for effect-foreign-other-entity (/Volumes/ssd/agent-data/claude/freeze-review/new-specimens-verify/probe_ns01.py and probe_ns01.out). The committed roe results carry BUDGET on all four effect decisions. A string scan finds 18 of 190 committed cases with EFFECT_OBSERVED that also contain a BUDGET kind, which matches the finding that the convention is corpus-wide. The gap was raised as READING in review/records/REVIEW-vectors-renewal-budget-20260912.md item 5, and neither CONTRACT-DECISIONS.md nor RESERVATION-GAPS-DECISION-20260913.md records a decision, so it is not a known item.

ra.txt 391-395: RA 2.3.1 (1) names PDSS and designated-status property as parties 'under your protection' whose endangerment justifies fire. It does not make a protected individual a barred target. RA 4.3 (ra.txt 728-732: a class result 'should be marked as an invalid target' when the RoE marks protected entities) is the passage that supports roe-02. MAPPING.md presents the nine obligations as 'the specimen's synthetic reading', which softens the error but does not make the cited basis correct. The attribution is wrong. The scenario roe-protected-status using protected_status PDSS carries the same misreading. This is a non-normative source citation and changes no consumer result, so minor rather than major.

The text chain holds. COMPOSITION.md:236 anchors on the occurred_at of the completed anchor occurrence. LIFECYCLE.md:223 says a timely matching success records the native event_time. LIFECYCLE.md:168 requires attempted_at <= event_time. LIFECYCLE.md:137 says attempted_at is no earlier than the permit issuance clock. So antibiotic-window runs from the alert's delivery time, which can never be earlier than the proposal clock. source-policy.json hour-one-bundle defines time zero as 'the alert's recorded recognition time'. The trace hides the difference: clock rev 1, attempt, acknowledgement, event_time and observed_at are all 08:00:00Z (valid-trace/requests.jsonl lines 2, 4, 5). correspondence-record.json has 28 residue rows: 27 UNSUPPORTED provision rows plus the EXCLUDED alert-window-cap row, and none covers this. README.md:9 and DERIVATIONS.md:37 say no time-zero mismatch residue exists. Minor, not major: a synthetic policy can reasonably treat the alert's native record time as its recorded recognition time, and the gap is limited to the delay between recognition and the alert's own delivery. It is still worth one residue row.

COMPOSITION.md:236 adds an elapsed declaration to the admitted activation instant, and LIFECYCLE.md:275 defines activation_instant as the selected clock's observed time at activation. The derived state after sepsis-effect-alert shows attending-acknowledgement with activation_instant 08:00:00Z and due 08:15:00Z. The page is dispatched at 08:02:00Z (valid-trace/requests.jsonl line 9, attempted_at). source-policy.json escalate-unacknowledged-page says 'within fifteen minutes of the page'. The construct measures from step activation, and a page proposed late in the window gets almost no acknowledgement time. correspondence-record.json maps 106 paths, including /deadlines/1, to escalate-unacknowledged-page. No residue row and no sepsis EXPOSED-RULES entry records the difference, while the roe specimen records its own activation-anchored deadline as E3. Real divergence between the specimen record and the construct, limited to the non-normative correspondence; no consumer result changes.

LIFECYCLE.md:275: if a successor's activation clock already satisfies its deadline, no successor is created and the instance records STOPPED/DEADLINE_ALREADY_DUE. That rule depends on due having been computed from time zero, so it confirms README.md:7 ('runs from time zero however late the step activates') rather than contradicting it. The sentence is about where the measurement starts, and a READY choice at or after 09:00 finding the deadline already due is that measurement at work. DERIVATIONS.md:60 already names DEADLINE_ALREADY_DUE for the valid trace. No scenario covers the late-activation stop, but that is a coverage note, not a contradiction. I ran no consumer probe.

scenarios/expectations.json method: 'Every judgment, state and digest was derived ... before either draft-2 implementation ran on these artifacts.' DERIVATIONS.md line 3 and line 5 make the same claim. DERIVATIONS.md:89 says the deadline-order reading was 'Recorded 2026-09-13 after the first comparison run showed both consumers placing the rows in this order', and README.md:15 describes the same sequence. EXPOSED-RULES.md:69 says the builder was corrected 'from the text ... not from consumer output'. That is a claim about the basis of the reading, not its timing, but together these statements contradict the blanket before-any-run claim for this one ordering. The committed order itself is not in question. Provenance wording only.

gb.txt 1995-2002 (GB 3.3.13) requires mechanisms that let LAWS operation be 'altered, interrupted, or stopped altogether', activated by 'operators—or even the system itself'. The second sentence of roe-06 is a system-activated stop: the occurrence stops and no dispatch may follow. GB 3.3.13 is a reasonable secondary basis for that, listed after the primary RA 2.3.1 requirement 3. It does not mention a direction timeout, but the basis column does not claim it does. A defensible citation choice, not a defect.

MAPPING.md section 1 opens: 'Each row names a reference-architecture component, the section that describes it'. The row 'Engagement count as a mission constraint | 5.7.2 (response priorities), 2.1.4' names no RA component. ra.txt 1348-1360 (5.7.2) lists configuration settings with no count or rate cap, and ra.txt 349-356 (2.1.4) has no count either. Only the roe-07 basis says 'synthetic bound'. The component table presents a synthetic constraint as an architecture component. Citation clarity only.

RA 4.6.1 (ra.txt 789-796) says that in ML-based systems 'modification may not be the best approach' because discarded data is lost to later components. RA 4.6.2 (ra.txt 811-812) says 'annotating the data instead of modifying it allows components to later make creative use of the data'. RA 4.6.3 does recommend combining the two, but the section clearly leans toward retention for ML systems. A row titled 'Annotating over modifying', mapped to the specimen's retention choice, is a fair paraphrase of that lean. No defect worth reporting.

LIFECYCLE.md LIFE-008 (a later revocation does not erase a committed permit, reservation, dispatch or effect) can be shown only by a revocation observed against a state holding those records. In variant 9 the revocation is observed on instance B's proposal. LIFE-006 precedence stops before the registry transition, so budget_results is [] and only B's state is returned. The supplied registry being unchanged holds for every authority withholding, with or without a revocation. It does not show that A's permit or completed occurrence stands, since neither is in the request. DERIVATIONS.md:65 concedes that revocation after a permit is not exercised. Yet expectations.json state_and_budget_consequence says 'so instance A's committed effect stands', and MAPPING.md's 'Rules of engagement as issued by command' row cites this scenario for a committed permit, settled reservation and completed occurrence standing. The evidence is overclaimed; no result bytes change.

findings.title: Access-card nested correspondence review is attributed to an independent reviewer who never accepted this subject, and it carries no proxy label
findings.text_citation: library/work-class-specification/1.0.0-draft.2/Specification.md line 53: 'Its nested accepted review has subject digest digest("correspondence-subject", correspondence_without_review)... Changed subjects require new evidence unless an explicit rule permits continued reliance.' LIFE-003 (LIFECYCLE.md line 28) requires that the correspondence record's nested review status is ACCEPTED.
findings.expected_from_text: An ACCEPTED nested review must be a review of the exact current correspondence subject. When no such review exists, the record either comes from a real review of this subject or is marked as a proxy. Supplier-payment marks it with reviewer_id synthetic:specimen-proxy-reviewer:20260913 and a README sentence saying no person reviewed it. Access-card should use the same kind of marking.
findings.evidence: The record's review has reviewer_id independent-specimen-review-agent-20260911, status ACCEPTED, subject sha256:8cbf9180e52c60bdb6f1e99f0fb6f7a044a2b4526e844b86cd8aee7f238667f3 over work class sha256:ce5a735f.... README line 11 (changed in this range) says: 'Its nested review is the 2026-09-11 independent specimen review, ACCEPTED with finding AC-REV-002 recorded.' The review that record points to (its provenance digest equals sha256 of review/ACCESS-CARD-SPECIMEN-INDEPENDENT-REVIEW-20260911.json, 7189c58f...) says something different. It bound correspondence subject a3915540... over work class 9b57d59f.... Its correspondence status is MECHANICALLY_COMPLETE_REVIEW_PENDING (json line 55), its overall status is ACCEPTED_WITH_ONE_EVIDENCE_STATUS_BLOCKER (line 112), and it lists AC-REV-001 as an open blocker. The subject then changed twice: to c7d21355... at 7ce93525 (pin change), then to 8cbf9180... at HEAD, after this range moved recorded_at from 12:00 to 11:50. Recomputation is in /Volumes/ssd/agent-data/claude/freeze-review/existing-specimens/life003-checks.txt and the inline output of the correspondence digest probe. Deployment still returns DEPLOYED because the check is mechanical. The practical harm is the apparatus record: it presents a pending, blocker-bearing review of a different subject as an accepted independent review of this one, which contradicts the plan's step-5 accounting.
findings.proposed_fix: Mark the access-card review the way supplier-payment is marked: reviewer_id synthetic:specimen-proxy-reviewer:20260913, empty or proxy finding_ids, and a provenance that does not name the 2026-09-11 review file. Rewrite README line 11 to say no accepted independent review exists for the current subject and that AC-REV-001 stays open until step 5. Alternatively, have an independent reviewer accept subject 8cbf9180... and bind that record.
